title: Two Sum
kidExplanation: You have coins with numbers on them, and a piggy-bank goal (the target). You want two coins whose numbers add up exactly to the goal. As you look at each coin, you ask: 'Did I already see the partner coin I need?'
plainProblem: Given a list of numbers and a target, return the indices of two different numbers that add up to the target. Exactly one solution exists. You may not use the same element twice.

thinkingSteps.title: Brute force idea
thinkingSteps.body: Try every pair of indices. Correct, but about n×n checks.

thinkingSteps.title: Why it is slow
thinkingSteps.body: Most pairs are useless. We redo a lot of adding.

thinkingSteps.title: Aha insight
thinkingSteps.body: For the number in my hand, I only need target − that number. If I remembered past numbers in a map, I can check instantly.

thinkingSteps.title: Better idea
thinkingSteps.body: Walk once. Store value → index in a hash map. When the needed partner is already stored, return both indices.

pattern.name: Hash set / hash map for seen items
pattern.whenToSpot: You need fast lookups of values you already saw.

solutions.python:
class Solution:
    def twoSum(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> List[int]:
        # Memory: number we saw → where we saw it (hash map)
        prevMap = {}  # val -> index

        # Look at each number with its index
        for i, n in enumerate(nums):
            # Partner we need so n + partner == target
            diff = target - n
            # Have we already seen that partner?
            if diff in prevMap:
                # Yes — return partner index and current index
                return [prevMap[diff], i]
            # No — remember this number for future partners
            prevMap[n] = i

complexity.timeReason: Each number is processed once with average O(1) map lookups.
complexity.spaceReason: The map may store every number until we find the pair.

edgeCases: The two numbers can be the same value at different indices (e.g. [3,3], target 6).
Answer indices can be in any order unless the problem says otherwise — here return the pair you find.
commonMistakes: Returning the values instead of the indices.
Building the whole map first when a one-pass map is enough (both work; one-pass is cleaner).
interviewTips: Start by stating the brute force, then upgrade to the hash map.
Write the invariant: 'map stores values I have already visited'.
Confirm there is exactly one answer so you can return immediately.

steps.caption: Need two numbers that sum to 9.

interviewApproachNotes: One-pass hash map is the interview gold standard: O(n) time, easy to explain. Sorting + two pointers loses original indices unless you track them — map is simpler here.
